extracted.intended_audience: Wikipedia editors and contributors (people deciding whether to create, keep, merge, or delete event articles)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing whether an event merits its own Wikipedia article, covering evidentiary and contextual criteria (coverage, impact, duration, scope, reliability) and procedural advice for handling breaking or future events. Includes examples, anti-patterns, and suggested alternatives to deletion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of notability (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: An event is presumed to be notable if it has lasting major consequences or affects a major geographical scope, or receives significant non-routine coverage that persists over a period of time. Coverage should be in multiple reliable sources with national or global scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This one-sentence summary appears at top of the page as the rule of thumb. It combines lasting effect, geographic scope, and persistence/diversity of coverage as the main pathways to notability.

rubrics_metrics.name: General notability guideline (WP:GNG)
rubrics_metrics.description: A topic (including an event) is presumed notable if it has received significant coverage in reliable sources that are independent of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use WP:GNG as a baseline: multiple independent reliable sources are required; mere popularity or fame is secondary. If coverage is shallow or merely reprints, the event may not meet this guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring historical significance / Lasting effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Events are probably notable if they have enduring historical significance or a significant lasting effect (for example, acting as a precedent or catalyst for legislation, social change, rebuilding after disasters, population shifts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Adam Walsh murder (led to legislation), Hurricane Katrina, 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake. It may take weeks or months to determine lasting effects; recent events with unproven lasting effect are not automatically non-notable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very likely notable: widespread impact or extensive re-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Events are very likely to be notable if they have widespread (national or international) impact or were very widely covered in diverse sources, especially if they are subsequently re-analyzed or used as case studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widespread impact or persistent scholarly/journalistic re-analysis strengthens notability beyond initial news spikes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Notable events usually have significant impact over a wide region, domain, or widespread societal group; events affecting only a local area and reported only in the immediate region may not be notable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National or international coverage increases likelihood of notability but should not be the sole basis. Events that demonstrably have long-term impact on a significant region or societal group are presumed notable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of coverage (significant/in-depth vs. in-passing)
rubrics_metrics.description: An event must receive significant or in-depth coverage to be notable; coverage must be more than passing or routine reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In-depth coverage includes books, feature-length magazine articles (Time, The New Yorker, etc.), and TV news specialty shows (60 Minutes, CNN Presents). Routine reporting that merely states facts without context is often insufficient. Beware sources that primarily reference older events — such pieces may not establish notability for the new event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of coverage / Persistence
rubrics_metrics.description: Notable events usually receive coverage beyond a relatively short news cycle; a burst or spike of reports is not alone sufficient to establish notability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage that continues, or later citations using the event as a case study, indicate lasting significance. Recent occurrence alone does not imply non-notability, but editors cannot assume lasting importance shortly after an event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and independence of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant national or international coverage from multiple independent sources is usually expected; sources that mirror each other or are under common control are discounted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple reports from the same newspaper/network or reprints of a single wire story generally do not count as independent sources. Media outlets under common ownership or stories simply re-reporting AP/press releases should be treated as one source for notability purposes (see Wikipedia:Bombardment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine coverage is not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine news coverage of scheduled or common events (announcements, sporting results, press conferences, wedding announcements, crime logs, etc.) is usually not a sufficient basis for a standalone article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planned events and promotional coverage are considered routine. Run-of-the-mill or novelty stories (e.g., 'bear-in-a-tree') usually lack lasting value and are probably not notable; such matters may be better covered within broader articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism and tabloid reporting are poor bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabloid-style, sensationalist, scandal-mongering or gossip reporting is usually a poor basis for an encyclopedia article because of lack of fact checking and emphasis on infotainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of 24-hour news cycle churn, churnalism, and media bias (e.g., 'missing white woman syndrome'). Refrain from creating articles rooted in scandal-mongering or gossip; apply BLP and other policies where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal acts: coverage may confer notability if reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles about criminal acts can be notable if media coverage meets the general notability and reliability guidelines; disappearance cases fall under this guideline if law enforcement treats them as likely crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an event is treated as notable and appears to be a crime, the article may remain even if later no crime is found (e.g., 'Runaway bride case'); ensure sources are reliable and coverage meets depth/duration/diversity tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: People notable only for one event
rubrics_metrics.description: People known only in connection with a single event should generally not have standalone biographical articles; if the event is notable, the article should usually be about the event instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful handling to avoid BLP violations and undue weight: merge or reframe biographies as event-focused articles where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future / anticipated events
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipated or scheduled future events may have articles only if they are verifiable and of sufficiently wide interest that they would merit an article if they had already occurred; they should be almost certain to take place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dates are not definite until the event happens; speculation without verifiable sources or original research is not appropriate. Preparation or documentation must be in progress to justify a pre-event article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking news: don't rush to create articles
rubrics_metrics.description: When an event is still being widely covered (breaking news), editors are advised not to rush to create separate articles; early coverage may lack perspective and be error-prone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended alternatives include starting a section within an existing related article which can be split later if warranted. Use {currentevent} template for ongoing coverage. Avoid creating standalone articles based solely on early, possibly inaccurate reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't rush to delete articles on breaking events
rubrics_metrics.description: Deletion nominations for breaking news items should normally be delayed a few days to allow the situation and notability to clarify; deletion debates during active coverage rarely reach consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives to immediate deletion include merging, reworking, preserving in draftspace, or 'userfying' while the story develops. Deletion while an event is still evolving can be counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to deletion / merging and reworking
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event's notability is in question, consider merging the content into a related article, reworking the article to broaden its context beyond a single incident, or keeping content in drafts/user space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When merging or reworking, avoid giving the event undue weight and observe biographies of living persons policy where applicable. If no merge target exists, broaden context rather than maintain a marginal standalone article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recentism: beware overvaluing recent events
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should be mindful of recentism — the tendency to treat new/current matters as more important than they may be historically — since news values differ from encyclopedic values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer measured judgment about long-term significance rather than immediate news prominence when deciding to create or retain articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting and treatment of derivative/chain reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative reports, wire-service reprints, and publications that merely re-report other outlets do not constitute multiplicity of independent sources and should be discounted when establishing notability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several journals republishing the same wire story are not multiple independent sources. Treat common-control outlets as a single source for notability; verify original reporting rather than counting echoes.
